It is to be noted that ensuring the Level 1 flying qualities in the closed-loop sense using
pole placement and SAS alone does not necessarily guarantee the Level 1 handling
qualities. Upon receiving the open-loop parameters, the control engineers will design
a complicated AFCS that operates robustly, considering the phase and gain margins,
as well as the Neal-Smith and Gibson dropback criteria.
100

The design of advanced flight control systems is considered beyond the scope of this
thesis, and hence, it is not covered here. Therefore, it can be argued that while the
flight mechanics engineer deals mainly with the flying qualities of the closed-loop
system to some extent, the control engineer will do the job on part of the handling
qualities by designing a full-envelope flight control system. The choice of the control
system might change from project to project. For instance, F-35 is known to employ
Nonlinear Dynamics Inversion (NDI) control law [175], while in some projects, a
simple PID would work. Of course, control engineers can use ADA to initiate the
control law studies in Simulink. However, it is better to wait until the full aerody-
namic database arrives. Depending on the type of controller, control engineers will
be able to reach state-space models and transfer functions, which are always available
through ADA.
It is known from the F-22 experience that the short-period mode design goals broke
down to the damping ratio and CAP of 0.8 and 1.0, respectively, as discussed by
Harris et al. [186]. In this study, the damping ratio of the short-period mode was
scheduled to always lie between 0.80 and 0.90, depending on the flight type and
condition. The CAP estimation is done conceptually, as discussed in Section 4.5.2.2,
and not enforced to become a value of 1.0, as followed in F-22. Depending on the
desired responsiveness of the aircraft, the control engineers shall tailor the closed-
loop gains to meet the Level 1 handling qualities. In that case, the damping of the
short-period root would stay about the same, while the frequency and the CAP would
change. Table 5.16 presents some stability derivatives attained in cruise.

5.3.2
Descent
As the pilot intends to land, the landing gears are extended, the flight path angle is set
to about -3 degrees, and the flight phase is called the landing approach. The limit air-
speed at which the landing gears are extended and retracted might significantly vary
for each aircraft, which is usually less than 300 KCAS, and this is mostly determined
later on as the full aerodynamic database is obtained and assessed by structural anal-
ysis. In ADA, flight path stability is analyzed for descent maneuvers since the flight
path angle is negative. Roskam [144] suggests that the minimum operating speed,
Vomin, is typically 1.20 times that of the powered-approach stall speed for land-based
aircraft. Abzug [76] notes that the linearized equations of motion befit for an air-
craft in cruise, climb, and landing approach since they are among the most linear
systems attainable during steady and symmetric flight. The descent maneuver flight
summaries to be assessed in terms of flight path stability are given in Table 5.17.

5.3.3
Pull-up
In a steady, symmetrical pull-up maneuver, the steady state pitch rate is the only angu-
lar rate [144, 189]. Though mathematically feasible, Napolitano [184] discusses that
completing the maneuver under the steady-state assumption is physically impossible
since the assumptions of zero linear & angular accelerations cannot be achieved in
the climbing and descending phases of the loop. Abzug [158] refers to this maneuver
as "quasi-steady" instead of steady since ˙u and ˙w cannot both remain at zero in the
long run. Stengel [189] notes that a steady pull-up modifies the lateral-directional
eigenvalues, and this phenomenon can also be verified by checking Equation 4.26.
Pamadi [121] discusses that the static stability level of the pull-up maneuver is higher
than that of level flight. However, this is only true for inherently statically stable
aircraft. Such examples are the F-14A and F-15B. In the case of RSS aircraft, the
Cmα vs α curve does not always follow an increasing or decreasing trend. Rather, it
constantly changes with respect to flight conditions (altitude, Mach, CG) and angle
of attack. Say for an AoA range of α1 and α2, the trim AoA for the cruise has been
calculated as αcruise. Since the required AoA to trim the aircraft at pull-up (nz > 1)
is greater than the level flight at the same altitude, CG, and speed conditions, the
required AoA at pull-up is found to be αpull-up > αcruise. If, between α1 and α2, the
Cmα vs α curve has the approximate form as in part (a) of Figure 5.14, then the static
& dynamic instability of the pull-up will be lower than the one at cruise whereas in
part (b), the instability level of the pull-up will be higher than that of the cruise.
(a) Decreasing Trend of Cmα vs α
(b) Increasing Trend of Cmα vs α
Figure 5.14: Possible Relative Instability in Cruise and Pull-up for RSS Aircraft
105

5.3.4
Coordinated Turn
The coordinated turn is not a maneuver that scholars agree upon its definition. The
MIL-STD-1797A [166] states that it can be achieved if ny is held zero during the
maneuver.
Schmidt [145] proposes that the following items all refer to coordinated turn, and
adds that they are not all equivalent: (i) The sideslip angle, β, is zero. (ii) The lateral
inertial acceleration of the vehicle CG is zero. (iii) The turn rate is constant with the
bank angle and flight velocity. (iv) The lateral acceleration at the cockpit is zero.
Phillips [183] proposes that in a perfectly coordinated turn, there must be no side
force. Adding that the term "steady" requires both the airspeed and angular velocity
to be constant. Additionally, the aircraft can be climbing or descending during a
coordinated turn.
Sadraey [182] follows the definition of Roskam. He explains that the coordinate turn
is a maneuver with zero aerodynamic side force and lateral acceleration. Thus, he
distinguishes the coordinated turn from the slipping and skidding turn. Thereby, he
permits a small amount of sideslip, as Roskam does, as long as the lateral acceleration
is kept zero.
Therefore, in this thesis, whenever a coordinated turn is mentioned, the following
items must be understood:
• The aerodynamic side force is kept at zero. (FAy = 0)
• The lateral acceleration is kept at zero. (ny = 0)
• A small amount of sideslip angle is permitted. (β is small)
• The aircraft maintains a constant speed, angular velocity, pitch, and bank angles
while the heading angle continuously changes at a constant rate. (V , p, q, r, θ,
ϕ, ˙ψ = const.) Also, ˙ϕ = ˙θ = 0.
• The aircraft might be climbing (γ > 0 and ˙h > 0) or descending (γ < 0 and
˙h < 0) in a coordinated turn. If the altitude is constant (γ = 0 and ˙h = 0)
during the maneuver, it is called the level coordinated turn.

In Table 5.26, it can be observed that the sign of feedback gains Kp and Kr do not
change in each case. This can also be observed throughout the thesis, where feedback
gains are presented. This is due to the fact that the stability derivatives Clp and Cnδr
have negative and positive signs, respectively. This phenomenon was also mentioned
in Sections 4.4.3.2 and 4.4.3.3. Another point to note is the relative magnitude of
the gain Kp with respect to Kr. This is due to the high moment of inertia about the
xb-axis of the aircraft, which results in a smaller roll mode eigenvalue. Consequently,
to correct for this sluggish open-loop pole in the closed-loop, the roll damper gain
has turned out to be of magnitude about 1 in some cases. In general, the smaller
the magnitude of the open-loop roll mode root, the bigger the closed-loop feedback
gain for the roll damper will be. This circumstance is usually observed in large and
heavy aircraft. The sensitivity analysis of the rolling moment of inertia, Ixx, on the
roll mode, can be found in Table F.8. The feedback control laws that are used in the
lateral-directional axis can be found in Table E.2.
As for the longitudinal feedback gains, it always occurred that the Ku, forward speed
to horizontal tail gain, is the smallest. This was expected since the forward speed
feedback to the horizontal tail is usually neglected in military aircraft. In the modern
Mach hold modes of the aircraft, the forward speed to throttle feedback, which is not
modeled in this study, is preferred. A summary of the longitudinal feedback laws
used in military aircraft to some extent can be found in Table E.1.

5.3.5
Steady Heading Sideslip
The steady heading sideslip is defined as a steady, straight flight that is not symmetric,
i.e., involving lateral motion variables, such as β and ϕ. Together with crabbing flight,
they constitute the landing approach flight phase maneuvers of fighter aircraft under
crosswind conditions. However, the SHSS maneuver is not only used in power ap-
proach mode (LG on). The fighters shall be able to conduct this maneuver at altitude
while climbing or descending, too. This is commonly referred to as the up-and-away
mode (LG off) of the fighter jets. The steady heading sideslip flight summaries for

5.3.6
Crab
Crabbing flights are mostly encountered during crosswind landing scenarios. As the
crosswind acts onto the landing runway from a side, the aircraft is "crabbed" to the
relative wind while maintaining the heading, hence canceling out the sideslip angle
by deflecting into-the-wind ailerons and opposite-rudder(s) to correct the drift. The
sideslip angle before establishing the trim is caused by the angle between the cross-
wind vector and the forward velocity vector of the aircraft. At the trim instant, the
sideslip angle is canceled out. Unlike SHSS, banking the aircraft to establish the trim
is not needed. Hence, aircraft flies wings-level in this type of maneuver. It is known
that [133, 190] the airliner pilots favor this type of landing to steady heading sideslip.
In the case of fighter jets, the final decision is up to the pilot, but the aircraft shall be
made suitable for both approaches. The crabbing flight summaries for each case are
presented in Table 5.32:

5.3.7
One Engine Inoperative
All types of aircraft might experience engine loss due to causes such as compres-
sor stall, in-flight icing, and foreign object damage (e.g., bird strike). This situation
might occur during takeoff and landing or once airborne. In the case of twin-engine
aircraft, the loss of one engine situation is called "one engine inoperative," or in short,
OEI. After an engine loss in a twin-engine aircraft, the inoperative engine produces
windmilling drag, adding an extra yawing moment on the aircraft. For a low BPR
jet-engine aircraft, the windmilling drag that the inoperative engine produces is about
15% of the normal thrust produced before it goes off, as suggested by Roskam [144].
Yechout et al. [122] suggest the interval of 10 to 15% for the windmilling drag.
In that case, the aircraft will tend to yaw toward the inoperative engine and to bank on
either side. The latter depends on the position of the inoperative engine’s own center
of gravity with respect to the aircraft’s center of gravity. If the center of gravity of the
operating engine is positioned below the center of gravity of the aircraft, the aircraft
will bank down on the side of the operating engine [191]. In this study, it is assumed
that the z-component of the center of gravity of the engines and the aircraft are at
the same level. Hence, no initial banking tendency will take place. This approach
was adopted in the first place since thrust asymmetry (or thrust line offset) along the
z-body axis would cause a thrust moment coefficient, CmT , which would complicate
the analyses.
In OEI trim conditions, the required β, δa, and δr are solved for a given bank angle,
ϕ, for which there is a special requirement. Per MIL-STD-1797A [166], it is stated
that the maximum bank angle during the trim for straight flight should not exceed 5
degrees away from the inoperative engine. For a right engine inoperative case, this
would mean that the bank angle ϕ is limited by -5 degrees. Schmidt [161] finds the
choice of 5 degrees rather arbitrary. However, he adds that it must have been proposed
to provide a sufficient ground clearance limit for low-wing, multi-engine aircraft. It is
suggested that the amount of rudder deflection to hold the trim at OEI conditions can
be significantly reduced if the aircraft is banked toward the operating engine [144].
Yechout et al. [122] narrate that pilots refer to this condition as "banking into the
good engine."
134

In the following analyses, it is assumed that the most critical engine is the one on
starboard, i.e., the right engine becomes inoperative. The analyses are conducted
such that after takeoff the right engine becomes inoperative while climbing upon the
retraction of landing gears. The windmilling engine is assumed to produce 15 % drag
of the normal thrust. The aircraft banks into the good engine to reduce the control
surface deflections required to hold the 1-g trim while establishing an SHSS. The
flight summaries are given in Table 5.35, which reflect distinct case studies.

Figure 5.40: OEI: Case 2 Sizing Plot

136

Figure 5.41: OEI: Case 3 Sizing Plot

From the sizing plots, it has been observed that at relatively low speeds, the rudder
alone cannot produce enough yawing moment to keep the trim at SHSS since the
dynamic pressure could not suffice, which was also reported by Russell [192], hence
the aileron quickly reacts to keep the trim at positive bank angles, as can be seen
in Figure 5.39, reaches its deflection limit, and thereby becomes the limiting factor.
Moreover, it is now quite understandable why the pilots prefer to bank into the good
engine for the control surface deflections and sideslip angle are minimum there.

CHAPTER 6
CONCLUSION
6.1
Conclusion
The primary purpose of this study was to show that the engineering analyses that lead
to controls from the first geometric concept can be systematically done using free
software in seconds. The results of the analyses are supplementary by-products that
stood up for this main purpose. To highlight the reasoning of the study, the adopted
methodology is discussed in detail. The implication of the controller design section
was found to be useful in the assessment of flying quality levels of the designed con-
ceptual aircraft since those requirements need to be met in the closed-loop sense.
During the process, the details of the designed aircraft were explained, and some
databases were provided to researchers. It has been put forth that a fifth-generation-
like aircraft in some aspects, e.g., outer geometry, relaxed static stability, static &
dynamic stability, mass & inertia, can be analyzed in terms of flight mechanics us-
ing Digital DATCOM only if the geometric information of the aircraft is available
via free modeling software such as OpenVSP. Those analyses were possible since a
design and analysis tool named ADA was developed in the preparation of this thesis.
The proprietary tool designed by the author made it possible to assess the aircraft’s
dynamic behavior for various maneuvers that all fighter jets inevitably perform. One
notable output that can also be stated here once again is that the employment of re-
laxed static stability made the aircraft statically and dynamically unstable. Hence,
the controller gains happened to be bigger compared to conventional, statically stable
fighters of the previous generations. Some of the databases, best practices, must-
knowns, sensitivity analyses, classifications, and definitions peculiar to the topic are
compiled in the Appendices for ease of referral.
139

It has also been shown that the design and analysis of a fifth-generation fighter jet
were possible thanks to the ADA, just as intended from the beginning. In modern
days, even the initial analyses need to be quick and should have some reliability.
Old-fashioned hand calculations do not seem to provide much to favor. Instead, com-
puterized tools must be consulted. These tools can either already exist and be taken
for granted, or the engineers might opt to design their proprietary tools for their own
specific needs. The latter approach was adopted in this study. Since it was a fifth-
generation fighter intended to be designed from the beginning, the outline of the pro-
gram was scheduled to meet its needs. This approach turned out to be more educative
than clicking on buttons in an already available, tested, and easy-to-learn software
designed to draw and analyze aircraft. Creating a need-oriented tool was also help-
ful in responding to the question of what a flight mechanics engineer wishes to see
beforehand in numerous outputs. This sound question is believed to be answered by
ADA and ADAdynamic GUI options, whereas the secondary outputs are sent to Ex-
cel and MAT-files. It should not be forgotten that the use of ADA shall be limited to
conceptual and preliminary studies only. However, it will always be ready to serve
to infer an idea. For instance, the engineers might find it more convenient to initially
assess the change in the stability derivative Cmq in case of a 20% reduction in the
area of the horizontal tail before consulting a CFD analysis. As the design matures,
the use of ADA will gradually decline as all other competing tools do. As the entire
aerodynamic database is generated for the matured aircraft, the need for preliminary
methods will tend to vanish. Indeed, tools like ADA are never intended to replace
the more advanced 6-DOF simulation methods, as Digital DATCOM never aimed to
substitute wind tunnel testing.
Overall, the author does not claim that the designed aircraft is superb, flyable, and
producible. The analysis results provided in Chapter 5 are valid only for the designed
aircraft for which the details are provided in Tables 5.3, 5.9 and so on when analyzed
using ADA only. From the beginning, the idea was to prove that these analyses could
be done, and they have shown to be done. Of course, this attempt is just a prelimi-
nary thought on the subject of fifth-generation fighters, and this study covered only
the flight mechanics perspective to some extent. Nevertheless, it is believed that a
standard has been set for further inquiries.
140

The following items summarize the conclusions drawn from this study:
• It has been shown that a need-oriented design and analysis tool might work
well on the analyses the researcher wishes to conduct by constantly adjusting
the code and adapting to any need that provides sufficient results in under ten
seconds. However, the preparation time to obtain reliable results almost takes a
year to achieve a confidence level.
• The relative importance scales presented in Tables F.2 and F.3 might guide the
researchers to estimate the significant stability derivatives better and save time
by not spending too much time on the estimation of relatively insignificant
derivatives if they wish to consult linear, decoupled dynamic models.
• Since unstable plants are fundamentally more difficult to control, conceptual
studies should set an upper limit for the maximum unstable short-period root.
Otherwise, the design will be constrained by actuator loads and the controller
gains are going to be bigger in order to meet Level 1 flying qualities.
• In the closed-loop sense, aircraft is made Level 1 using simple controller logic.
Using advanced controllers during the conceptual design would take much
more time since the design will be subject to change several times. Therefore,
advanced handling quality criteria can be considered a secondary or tertiary
step to Level 1 qualities at the early conceptual design phase.
• As foreseen by esteemed scholars, it has become clear that in the analysis
of RSS aircraft, most of the time, the conventional phugoid and short-period
modes are absent in the open-loop; rather, a third-oscillatory mode is to be
found and the accompanying modes can either be named aperiodic divergent
phugoid mode and aperiodic convergent short-period mode or unstable short-
period mode and aperiodic convergent short-period mode. Moreover, due to the
small value of the Mach tuck derivative, Cmu, the tuck mode was not observed.
• In the maneuver analyses, never it has occurred that a coupled roll-spiral mode
was present. Ensuring this was also significant, since among all the possible
dynamic modes, it is the unwanted one.
141

6.2
Future Work
It is believed that many more detailed studies will follow, which might enrich the
common knowledge on the topic. These ideas are summarized as future work in what
follows:
• As the aerodynamic database is obtained for the full flight envelope, the LEF
and TEF schedules can be determined and used for initial assessments, which
could relax the demand on the aileron, rudder, and horizontal tail.
• ADA might be adjusted to work in cooperation with OpenVSP. Hence, the full
untrimmed aerodynamic database may be obtained for all flight regimes. Thus,
the 6-DOF equations of motion can be solved for each maneuver. If that can
be achieved, the full envelope AFCS might be designed based on the outputs of
ADA using Simulink.
• If a real or specifically designed engine deck is integrated into ADA, as de-
signed by GasTurb or elsewhere, the performance module can also be added.
Thus, the full envelope performance analyses can be completed. Those analyses
might include range, endurance, SEP, and turn performance charts. Therefore,
point, mission, and field performance evaluations can be performed.
• Future updates of ADA might include a cost module to estimate the engineering
and production costs, just as AAA and RDS do. A history module is also fea-
sible to store the data and show when necessary how the previous aircraft such
as F-4, F-15, and F-16 behaved at similar weight, CG, and speed conditions.
• With a better and refined aerodynamic database, it shall become possible to
conduct the uncertainty analyses of stability derivatives to see the effect on dy-
namic modes. To attain such a database, the aerodynamic outputs of OpenVSP
and a simple Euler code can be blended.
• As the conceptual design is matured and more details are uncovered, the weight
and inertia could be directly taken from OpenVSP using real materials such as
aluminum, titanium, steel, and composites, which could enhance the overall
accuracy of the analyses.

APPENDIX B
STABILITY DERIVATIVES FOR EACH GENERATION
This appendix is dedicated to presenting the nondimensional and dimensional stabil-
ity derivatives of each generation of fighter jets, as far as the sources allow.
As previously discussed in Section 5.2.4, every other scholar uses distinct sign con-
ventions. Hence, when in doubt about the sign of a particular stability derivative,
Table 5.6 can be referred to review the sign convention used by other authors.
The significance of stability and control derivatives cannot be overemphasized. In the
course of the conceptual design of any aircraft, the stability derivatives of existing and
similar aircraft are sought. What is sought is a trend rather than the derivative itself,
as shown in Figures 5.12 and 5.13, though the derivatives might also become useful
to infer initial ideas for conducting the trade studies. For instance, the magnitude
of the stability derivative Clp should not significantly change for F-15 and any fifth-
generation fighter jet due to shape and size similarities.
Tables B.1 and B.2 include the nondimensional stability derivatives, whereas Table
B.3 is a collection of dimensional stability derivatives. Presenting the dimensional
stability derivatives as in Table 5.6 might seem a vague comparison since they include
the mass, inertia, and size effects, though they are heavily used to derive the aircraft
transfer functions, which is the objective of incorporating them.
A greater spectrum of stability derivatives for various aircraft types can be found in
the work of McRuer et al. [129], Roskam [144], Heffley et al. [137], and Teper [160].
Note that the derivatives given in Tables B.1, B.2, and B.3 are all in the stability axes.
The reader is always kindly reminded to refer to Appendix F whenever a doubt arises
about the sign and meaning of a particular derivative.

APPENDIX C
ESTIMATION OF UNSTABLE SHORT-PERIOD ROOT
Oftentimes, it is the unstable short-period root that drives the longitudinal control
characteristics of the aircraft having relaxed static stability in the longitudinal axis.
Hence, even with limited knowledge of the nondimensional stability derivatives, it is
sought to compute the unstable short-period root location for different kinds of ma-
neuvers such as cruise, pull-up, and coordinated turn at distinct altitudes to understand
the closed-loop gain demand on the longitudinal stability and control augmentation
system (SCAS). An approximation to the short-period mode of the aircraft makes it
possible for the estimation of unstable short-period root location as given in Etkin
[120]. The approximate root location, after a little algebra, can be found as:

APPENDIX F
DISCUSSION OF NONDIMENSIONAL STABILITY DERIVATIVES
Nondimensional stability derivatives find extensive use in flight mechanics and con-
trol applications. Therefore, designers should have a good fundamental grasp of them.
In this section, longitudinal and lateral-directional nondimensional stability deriva-
tives are somewhat discussed.
Longitudinal Nondimensional Stability Derivatives
CLu represents the change of lift coefficient with variations in forward velocity [129].
It arises due to Mach number and aeroelastic effects. Its magnitude is usually negli-
gible for low subsonic flight but it can reach a considerable value around the critical
Mach number of the aircraft [129]. Its value is positive for subsonic flow, but it can
change sign in transonic flow and is negative for supersonic flow [141]. It enters into
dynamic stability as a parameter in the frequency of the phugoid mode [141]. It is not
considered as a design parameter.
CDu corresponds to an increase of drag with an increase in speed [141] and is called
speed damping derivative [122, 127]. It can arise due to Mach number and aeroe-
lastic effects [129], where the latter is usually small and can be neglected. Its value
is usually neglected for subsonic Mach numbers. However, in the transonic region
(0.8<M<1.2), it is usually positive, indicating a substantial drag rise. For the super-
sonic region, its value is mostly negative [122]. (Please refer to drag vs Mach number
curves of fighters). It enters into dynamic stability as a parameter in the damping of
the phugoid mode. It is mostly regarded as a performance parameter rather than a
design parameter [141]. This derivative is one of the reasons why World War II-era
aircraft could not break the sound barrier, as more drag required more thrust.
177

Cmu represents the change in the pitching moment due to variations in the forward
speed [83]. Its value mostly depends on the Mach number and aeroelastic effects
[83, 129]. In the transonic region below the speed of sound, this derivative is nega-
tive, which implies that the aircraft has a tendency to put the nose down, also referred
to as "tuck under", hence the name: Mach tuck derivative [122, 130, 141, 144]. Pos-
itive values of this derivative increase static stability [141]. For the low aspect ratio
supersonic fighter designs of the latest generation, this derivative may be small over
the entire speed range [141], compared to previous generation jet fighters. The damp-
ing ratio and the frequency of the phugoid mode are affected by its value [144]. The
designer usually has little control over its value.
CLα represents the change in lift coefficient with a change in angle of attack and is
commonly known as "the lift curve slope" [129, 130, 141]. As the angle of attack is
increased, the lift coefficient will increase up to the stall angle of attack. Therefore,
this derivative is always positive below the stall angle of attack. The total airframe
CLα is made up of contributions of the wing, fuselage, and horizontal tail, where the
wing contribution is around 80 to 90 percent of the total value [129, 130]. Lower
values of this derivative will result in a relatively higher angle of attack at takeoff and
landing. It contributes to the damping and frequency of the short-period mode and is
mostly a performance-driven parameter rather than flight mechanics.
CDα is the representation of a change in drag coefficient with a change in angle of
attack. Its sign is positive in the positive range of attack angle and mostly depends
on aspect ratio and Oswald efficiency factor [122]. A decrease in CDα increases the
damping of the phugoid slightly. It is not considered as a design parameter. However,
from a performance point of view, it ought to be as small as possible [141].
Cmα represents the change in pitching moment coefficient with angle of attack and
is usually referred to as "longitudinal static stability derivative" or "pitch stiffness pa-
rameter". Its sign and magnitude are eminently affected by the location of the center
of gravity [130] and tail size [141], respectively. It is a primary design parameter for
static margin, static stability, and the frequency of the short-period mode. Its sign
is negative for longitudinally statically stable aircraft, and it changes sign over the
attainable angle of attack range for RSS aircraft as discussed in Section 4.2.1.1.
178

CL ˙α is the change in lift coefficient with rate of change of angle of attack. It arises
mostly due to the aerodynamic time lag of the horizontal tail [143], and various dead-
weight aeroelastic effects [129]. Its sign is positive in the subsonic flow regime but
might become negative in the supersonic region. The effect of this derivative on longi-
tudinal dynamic modes is usually insignificant and hence often neglected in dynamic
analyses [129, 143]. However, if available, it enters Equation 4.16 in the form of Z ˙α.
CD ˙α is the variation of the drag coefficient with the angle of attack rate at a constant
pitch rate [143]. For most practical applications, the lag in downwash has a negligi-
ble effect on the drag coefficient [122], and this derivative is often neglected [87] in
dynamic analyses. See Table F.2.
Cm ˙α is produced by the same effects of CL ˙α [122, 129]. Though CL ˙α is usually
negligible in dynamic analysis, Cm ˙α is quite important since it directly affects the
damping of the short-period mode [129, 130] and is negative in sign. The designers
have little control over this derivative since it is usually determined by configuration
setup. Too low a value of this derivative may stall and crash the aircraft after a plung-
ing motion [182]. For fighter jets, this derivative is usually about half or more of the
pitch damping derivative, Cmq, in magnitude. Please refer to Tables B.1 and B.2.
CLq is the variation of lift coefficient with pitch rate and its sign is positive. As with
CL ˙α, the effect of CLq on longitudinal dynamic stability is generally very small and
usually neglected in dynamic analyses [129, 143]. However, if available, it enters
Equation 4.16 in the form of Zq.
CDq is the variation of drag coefficient with pitch rate. For most practical applica-
tions, this derivative is very small and hence neglected [87, 122, 129].
Cmq is the variation of pitching moment coefficient with pitch rate and is often re-
ferred to as "pitch damping derivative," Its sign is often negative for both stable and
unstable aircraft configurations [140]. It is considered a primary design parameter
and is directly linked to the damping of the short-period mode [122, 141]. Adequate
values of this derivative are therefore needed for good handling qualities for the entire
flight envelope. However, less negative values of this derivative are found to be ac-
ceptable for high-performance fighters since AFCS provides artificial damping [140].
179

CLδe is the variation of lift coefficient with elevator (all-moving HT for 5th genera-
tion, CLit) deflection. Its sign is positive with the convention used in this study, as
the positive (trailing-edge-down) deflection of the elevator produces more lift. For an
all-moving horizontal tail, it is understood that CLit is meant.
CDδe is the variation of drag coefficient with elevator (all-moving HT for 5th genera-
tion, CDit) deflection. This derivative is usually neglected by most scholars [83, 122,
129], though estimation through the Digital DATCOM output file is quite straightfor-
ward. The sign of this derivative can be either positive or negative, depending on the
trim position of the horizontal tail and the trim angle of attack [129]. Generally, it is
the least important control derivative of longitudinal motion.
Cmδe is the variation of pitching moment coefficient with elevator (all-moving HT
for 5th generation, Cmit) deflection and often referred to as "elevator control power
derivative" [83, 122] or "elevator control effectiveness" [130, 140]. Its sign is neg-
ative with the sign convention used in this study for positive (trailing-edge-down)
deflection of the elevator creates a negative pitching moment. It is a primary design
parameter to ensure adequate elevator deflection to trim the aircraft in the entire flight
envelope. Its significance is most appreciated during the takeoff rotation and landing
approach [182]. This derivative is simply equivalent to Cmit for the all-moving hori-
zontal tail [141]. For fighters that have close values of mean aerodynamic chord and
horizontal tail moment arm, the magnitude of CLδe and Cmδe are almost the same. It
is the most important control derivative of longitudinal motion.
Lateral-Directional Nondimensional Stability Derivatives
Clβ is the lateral static stability derivative which is often referred to as "dihedral
effect" [182, 201] or "effective dihedral" [129, 130]. It represents the change of the
rolling moment derivative with a small change in the angle of the sideslip [140]. It
is considered one of the most significant parameters of the aircraft [141]. Its sign
may be negative or positive for stable and unstable configurations, as discussed in
Section 4.2.2, though unstable configurations are much less frequently encountered.
It is involved in the damping of both Dutch roll and spiral modes [129, 130]. Larger
values of this derivative make the spiral mode more stable [202]. Its magnitude should
be about half that of Cnβ at subsonic and about equal to it at transonic speeds [23].
180

Cyβ represents the change in side force coefficient with sideslip angle at constant
angle of attack. Its normal sign is usually negative for practical configurations, i.e., the
side force opposes the sideward motion [129], implying that it positively contributes
to lateral-directional stability [182]. Small values of this derivative are undesired
since it makes coordinated turn difficult to achieve [130]. This derivative contributes
to the damping of the Dutch roll mode. The major contribution to its value comes
from the vertical tail [122, 129].
Cnβ is the variation of yawing moment coefficient with sideslip angle. It is generally
referred to as "directional static stability derivative," though "weathercock stability"
[130] and "yaw stiffness derivative" [182] are also used. It is considered one of the
most significant design parameters of the aircraft [141]. The designer can control this
derivative by changing the vertical tail size and position. The natural frequency of
Dutch roll mode is extensively governed by this derivative [140, 202]. It also affects
the stability of the spiral mode [130, 201]. The magnitude of Cnβ significantly drops
at high angles of attack and during supersonic flight. This problem led the designers
of second-generation fighter jets of the U.S. to use ventral fins to increase directional
stability, with the F-104 as the most prominent [203].
Clp is the change in rolling moment coefficient with the change in rolling velocity. It
is usually called "roll damping derivative" [182], and its sign is always negative [130]
unless the wing is stalled. As a primary design parameter, it directly affects the roll
mode eigenvalue, design of the ailerons, and maximum rolling velocity of the aircraft
in conjunction with Clδa. Artifical damping is provided to its value by roll dampers.
Cyp is the variation of side force coefficient with roll rate. Its sign can be positive
or negative, depending on the location of the vertical tail, the angle of attack, and
the sidewash from the wing [129]. Flight mechanics engineers commonly neglect
this derivative since it is of little importance in lateral-directional dynamic stability
analyses [129, 143, 144, 182]. See Tables B.1 and F.3.
Cnp is a cross-derivative that tends to couple rolling and yawing motions. Its sign is
usually negative, though a positive value is desirable since it increases the damping
of the Dutch roll mode [130, 201]. The effect of this derivative on lateral-directional
dynamics is often weak as it is mostly a small negative value [133]. See Table B.1.
181

Clr is a cross derivative that tends to couple yawing and rolling motions. Its sign is
usually positive for subsonic and negative for supersonic speeds [141]. Though it is
of secondary importance in lateral-directional dynamics, the positive values of this
derivative should be as small as possible for good spiral stability [129]. Its effect on
the damping of Dutch roll mode is of less importance [129, 130]. It is usually not
under the control of the designer. The trends in Figures 5.12 and 5.13 are common.
Cyr represents the variation of side force coefficient with yaw rate. Its sign is often
positive. It is a common practice, just as with Cyp, to neglect this derivative since its
contribution to lateral-directional dynamics is of little importance [129, 182].
Cnr represents the variation of yawing moment coefficient with yaw rate and is gener-
ally called as "yaw damping derivative". Its sign is almost always negative [122, 130],
thus contributing to dynamic directional stability [182]. It affects the damping of the
Dutch roll mode majorly, and more negative values of this derivative increase the
spiral mode stability. Usually, the designer is not in much control of its magnitude,
except for vertical tail size, which might be dictated by various other design consid-
erations [141]. Usually, high-performance fighters artificially augment this derivative
with the use of yaw dampers.
Clδa represents the change of rolling moment coefficient with aileron deflection and
is most commonly referred to as "aileron control power derivative" [122, 182] or
"aileron effectiveness" [129, 130, 141]. Per the convention used in this study, the sign
of this derivative is positive since left-aileron-down and right-aileron-up deflections
produce a right-wing-down rolling moment. Together with Clp, it establishes the
maximum roll rate of an aircraft [129], which is the sizing factor of ailerons.
Cyδa is almost always negligible [129, 130] during conceptual design, and there is no
practical means to estimate it effectively without the use of wind tunnel [87, 144].
Cnδa is a cross control derivative and called "adverse aileron yaw effect" when its sign
is negative since it tends to yaw the airplane to the opposite direction of the intended
turn [144]. When its sign is positive, it produces favorable or "proverse yaw" in turn
maneuvers [129]. Large values of either sign aggravate the lateral handling qualities.
Ideally, its value should be as small as possible for each sign, or zero if possible.
182

Clδr represents the generation of the rolling moment as a result of deflecting the rud-
der, and it is a cross control derivative. In conjunction with the sign convention used
in this study, a positive (trailing-edge-left) rudder deflection will normally produce
a positive side force, hence a positive rolling moment since the rudder is usually lo-
cated above the xb-axis of the aircraft [122, 129]. Consequently, its sign is normally
positive but small in terms of magnitude. The sign change can occur depending on the
AoA. From a flight mechanics perspective, positive values of this derivative tend to
roll the aircraft in the opposite direction of the turn maneuvers and act as an "adverse
rudder roll effect," so to speak. Practically, this derivative is of minor importance in
the dynamic lateral control of the aircraft and thus sometimes neglected [129, 201].
Cyδr represents the variation of side force coefficient as a result of deflecting the
rudder. In conjunction with the sign convention used in this study, a positive rudder
deflection (trailing-edge-left) produces a positive side force; hence, this derivative is
positive in sign. Its magnitude is mostly determined by the size, aspect ratio, and
sweepback of the vertical tail [122]. Its importance arises for OEI control.
Cnδr represents the change in yawing moment coefficient that results from rud-
der deflection and is usually referred to as the "rudder control power derivative"
[83, 122, 182] or "rudder effectiveness" [129, 130, 141]. It is negative in sign be-
cause a positive rudder deflection (trailing-edge-left) results in a negative yawing
moment. The requirements of counteracting adverse yaw to achieve a coordinated
turn, crosswind takeoff and landings, trimming the aircraft in one engine inoperative
(asymmetric thrust) situations, and spin recovery control [83, 129, 201] are the main
design drivers of this derivative which signify its importance. This derivative also
plays a part in determining the minimum control speed of the aircraft in asymmetric
thrust conditions, i.e., higher negative values of Cnδr decreases the minimum control
speed. Therefore, for a given takeoff speed, engine thrust, and engine y-moment arm,
the ability of the aircraft to trim in one engine inoperative condition depends majorly
on the magnitude of this derivative [144]. Thus, it is understood that this derivative is
one of the primary design parameters of the aircraft [141].
Note: In the transonic region, control derivatives rapidly lose effectiveness. About
half or more of the control effectiveness will be lost in the supersonic region.
183

Aerodynamic Coefficients
CL is defined as the lift coefficient of the total airframe. It is not referred to as
a stability derivative but rather an aerodynamic coefficient, even though it enters the
longitudinal dynamics (in Xα and Zu) at the trim condition. By definition, it is always
measured perpendicular to the relative wind and is positive in sign upward [129]. Low
values of CL are associated with low angles of attack and high speed, whereas high
values of it are associated with high angles of attack and low speeds. Its effect on
phugoid mode is obvious, but its value is always driven by performance considera-
tions rather than flight mechanics. The stall speed of the aircraft is a direct function
of the maximum value of CL. CLmax can be substantially increased by HLDs [204].
For fighters equipped with LEFs and TEFs, a maximum usable combat lift coefficient
of about 1.0-1.5 is attainable [23]. F-22A is reported to have a CLmax of 1.48 [205].
CD is defined as the drag coefficient of the total airframe. By definition, it is always
measured along the direction of the relative wind [129]. Though not referred to as
a stability derivative, it is the main contributor to the dimensional stability derivative
Xu, and it slightly contributes to the value of Zα at trim condition. The value of Xu
will be dominated by the trim value of airframe drag coefficient at low subsonic Mach
numbers. From a designer’s perspective, which is usually performance-driven, reduc-
ing the total airframe drag coefficient is regarded as art. As far as the performance
of an aircraft is concerned, it is one of the most important parameters; therefore, a
desirable value of CD is one that is as small as possible [156]. Its value may be lower
at supersonic speeds than in the transonic range, although it is surely higher than the
subsonic range [141].
Cm is defined as the aerodynamic pitching moment coefficient of the total airframe
about the center of gravity required to balance the moment coefficient due to thrust
(CmT = TzT/qS¯c) when the aircraft is at trim [129, 156]. It is not regarded as a
stability derivative, though it appears in Mu. The sign of Cm is positive if the line of
thrust is above the CG and negative if the line of thrust is below the CG. Its trim value
will be zero if the thrust moment arm is zero. In general, there will be a nonzero Cm
in the case of thrust offset. Nonzero values of Cm primarily affect the phugoid mode.
However, its importance in airframe dynamics is not well established [156].

Coupled Roll-Spiral Mode Sensitivity Analysis
When the aperiodic roll and spiral modes couple, the lateral-directional characteristic
equation takes the following factored form:
(s2 + 2ζdrωdr + ω2
dr)(s2 + 2ζrsωrs + ω2
rs) = 0
(F.1)
where the subscripts dr and rs denote Dutch roll and coupled roll-spiral modes, re-
spectively. The second term in parenthesis represents an unconventional, unwanted
complex conjugate root that describes a long period (T > 20 sec) oscillation, also
known as the lateral-phugoid [165], which can be brought about in the presence of:
(i) unusually large or small values of a particular stability derivative
(ii) a combination of several stability derivatives
These possibilities are better explained in Table F.6. It is reported that a coupled roll-
spiral mode can occur if an aircraft has low Clp and Cnβ in the presence of a high Clβ
for which the magnitude of Cnp should also be considered [162]. Note that too high
a value of Cnr will cause all lateral-directional roots to be aperiodic.

Table F.9 comprehensively summarizes the nondimensional stability derivatives with
subfamilies. It brings new discussions and several points to note.
Of the static stability derivatives, CDα and Cyβ are mostly overlooked as they do not
imply much by themselves. Moreover, often it is forgotten that the derivative Cyβ is
a static stability derivative, even though by all means it is. Static speed derivatives
are meaningful only for the longitudinal motion if it is decoupled from the lateral-
directional motion, which is usually the case for linearized analysis; otherwise, one
can also form the speed derivatives for lateral-directional motion. Longitudinal ac-
celeration derivatives are previously discussed in this chapter. The lateral-directional
counterparts of these derivatives are usually insignificant for linearized analysis.
Among the damping derivatives, CDq is the least important, and it is a common prac-
tice to neglect Cyp and Cyr in lateral-directional dynamic analysis, as noted earlier
in this chapter. Cross-coupling, or in short cross-derivative, is encountered only in
lateral-directional motion whenever the yawing motion tends to couple with rolling
motion and vice versa. The control derivatives Cnδa and Clδr are sometimes confi-
dently called cross-control derivatives. One should note that the presence of LEFs,
TEFs, and any other control surfaces will beget their control derivatives such as Cmδtef
and Cnδlef which are not shown in Table F.9 for the sake of brevity.

APPENDIX H
DEFINITION OF FLIGHT
It is to the advantage of flight mechanics engineers to understand the definitions of
different types of flight, as discussed what follows.
Steady Flight is defined as flight with zero rates of change of the linear and angular
velocity variables [126, 127, 144, 158], i.e., ˙u = ˙v =
˙w = ˙p = ˙q = ˙r = 0.
This implies that [u, v, w, p, q, r] = const. during the steady flight. Steady flight is
achieved with constant linear velocities, constant angular velocities, and constant load
factor. Steady level flight, steady sideslips, steady turns, and steady pull-ups are some
steady flight examples.
Straight Flight is defined as flight with zero angular velocity components [123, 158],
i.e., p = q = r = pw = qw = rw = 0. This implies that the aircraft is not turning
relative to the Earth [123]. Steady sideslips, steady rectilinear flight, dives, and climbs
with or without longitudinal acceleration are some straight flight examples.
Symmetric Flight is defined as flight with a fixed, vertical position of the plane of
symmetry. The variables p, r, ϕ, and v remain zero [158]. This type of flight includes
the following maneuvers with zero sideslip (β = 0): cruise, climb, descent, pull-up,
and push-over. In general, longitudinal motions are symmetric.
Asymmetric Flight is defined as flight in which the plane of symmetry does not
remain in a fixed vertical position. Some or all of the motion variables p, r, ϕ, and v
may be expected to be other than zero [158]. This type of flight includes the following
maneuvers: steady heading sideslip (SHSS), crab, OEI, aileron roll, barrel roll, and
turns (slipping turn, skidding turn, coordinated turn). In general, maneuvers involving
lateral motion variables are asymmetric.

COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES: 
At the end of this course, a student should be able to: 
• 
To learn and understand the concepts of operating system. 
• 
To understand the core structure and functions of operating system. 
• 
Explain process management, processor scheduling, and concurrent programming. 
• 
Understand the concept of deadlocks and synchronization. 
• 
Learn memory management, file management. I/O systems, and disk scheduling. 
• 
Distinguish main memory and virtual memory. 
• 
Leam Operating System Design issues. 
• 
Leam basic Unix commands and shell programming 
 
UNIT-1 (15 HOURS) 
Introduction: Goals & Structure of Operating System. Basic functions & Modes. Types of Operating System (Batch, 
Multiprogramming, Multitasking, Time Sharing, Parallel, Distributed A Real-Time OS). System calls. 
 
Process: Process Concept, Process states, Threads, Uni-processor Scheduling: Types of scheduling (Pre-emptive & 
Non- pre-emptive).  Scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SJF, RR, Priority, Thread Scheduling). 
 
UNIT-2 (15 HOURS) 
Concurrency: Principles of Concurrency, Mutual Exclusion: Software approaches, Hardware Support, Semaphores, 
Message Passing, Signals. Monitors, Classical Problems of Synchronization (Readers-Writers, Producer-Consumer, 
and Dining Philosopher problem). 
 
Deadlock: Principles of Deadlock. Deadlock Prevention & Avoidance, Deadlock Detection. 
 
UNIT-3 (15 HOURS) 
Memory: Memory Management requirements, Memory partitioning (Fixed and Variable Partitioning), Memory 
Allocation Strategies (First Fit, Best Fit and Worst Fit), Fragmentation. Swapping, Segmentation, Paging. 
 
Virtual Memory: Virtual Memory Concepts and Implementation, Concept of Demand Paging, Page Replacement 
Policies (FIFO, LRU, Optimal, Other Strategies). Thrashing.

Hot-Mix Asphalt Railroad Trackbeds 
YANG H. HUANG, JERRY G. ROSE, AND CHARLES J. KHOURY 
Since 1981 about 30 experimental sections of bot-mix asphalt 
trackbeds have been built and evaluated. The bot-mix asphalt 
can be used either as an overlay placed directly under the tie or 
as an underlay placed under the ballast. Because of the sim-
ilarity between highway pavements and railroad trackbeds, 
the concept deveioped ior the design oi highway pavements is 
investigated and extended to the design of hot-mix asphalt 
trackbeds. The design Is based on two criteria: limiting the 
horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of the hot-mix asphalt to 
prevent fatigue cracking and limiting the vertical compressive 
stress on the top of the subgrade to reduce permanent defor-
mation. The use of vertical compressive stress, instead of verti-
cal compressive strain, is a deviation from highway practice 
that is found to be more applicable to railroad trackbeds. A 
computer program based on the finite element method and 
Burmister's layered theory was developed for the design and 
analysis of asphalt trackbeds. The results of analysis show that 
underlays are far superior to overlays from a structural view-
point. Because of the difference In load distribution, an 
increase in the thickness of hot-mix asphalt is not as effective in 
reducing the stresses and strains In railroad trackbeds as it is 
in highway pavements. In designing underlays, the use of a 
thin layer of hot-mix asphalt and a thick layer of ballast is 
recommended. The main function of hot-mix asphalt under-
lays is to waterproof the subgrade, thus providing consistent 
load-carrying capability for the trackbed even on subgrades of 
marginal quality. The hot-mix asphalt mat will separate the 
ballast from the subgrade, confine the ballast, and eliminate 
pumping without substantially Increasing the stiffness of the 
trackbed. 
Although hot-mix asphalt (HMA) has been used for the con-
struction of highway pavements for more than a century, its use 
in railroad trackbeds is relatively new and is still in the experi-
mental stage. The first recorded use of hot-mix asphalt for 
railroad trackbeds in the United States was in 1968 when the 
Cleveland Transit Authority placed two 1,000-ft (305-m) 
asphalt test sections on a line extension near the airport (1 ). The 
westbound section had 5 in. (127 mm) of hot-mix asphalt, the 
eastbound 4 in. (102 mm), and the asphalt mats were placed 
directly on the subgrade and topped with 8 in. (203 mm) of 
baiiast. In i969 the Santa Fe Raiiway piaced three 700-ft (2i5-
mm) asphalt test sections on a new line to service a coal-mining 
region in northeastern New Mexico (2). The asphalt mats were 
2.5 in. (63 mm), 5 in. (127 mm), and 7.5 in. (190 mm) thick, 
respectively, and were placed under a 10-in. (254-mm) ballast. 
In spite of the excellent performance of these experimental 
sections, little work was done on hot-mix asphalt trackbeds 
until 1981 when a research project was initiated at the Univer-
sity of Kentucky under the joint financial support of the 
National Asphalt Pavement Association and the Asphalt 
Institute. The overall objective of this research is to evaluate 
and document the technical and economic benefits of railroad 
Department of Civil Engineering, University of Kentucky, Lexington,

trackbeds containing a layer of dense-graded hot-mix asphalt. 
With the cooperation of several railway companies, approx-
imately 30 different installations of asphalt trackbeds under a 
variety of traffic, soil, and environmental conditions have been

mances of these test trackbeds to develop a rational method for 
the design of hot-mix asphalt trackbeds. It is the purpose of this 
paper to describe the design, construction, and performance of 
hot-mix asphalt trackbeds with particular emphasis on the 
design differences between highway pavements and railroad 
trackbeds. 
CONSTRUCTION AND PERFORMANCE 
Two methods have been used to incorporate hot-mix asphalt in 
railroad trackbeds. One method, which is similar to the con-
struction of highway pavements, is to place the hot-mix asphalt 
on top of the sub grade or above a layer of base course. The ties 
are then placed directly on the asphalt mat. This type of 
construction is called full depth if the asphalt mat is built 
directly on the subgrade or overlay if a layer of granular base is 
used. The geometry of full depth and overlay is similar to that 
of highway pavements except that wheel loads are transmitted 
through rails and ties over a large area on the asphalt mat 
instead of through tires over small areas. Another method is to 
place the asphalt mat under the ballast. The asphalt mat actu-
ally serves as a subballast. For heavy-tonnage main lines on a 
poor subgrade, a granular base course or other stabilized mate-
rials may be placed between the hot-mix asphalt and the sub-
grade. This type of construction is called underlay and is 
preferred by railroad engineers because conventional railroad 
maintenance procedures can still be applied. Figure 1 shows 
typical cross sections for hot-mix asphalt trackbeds. 
When the asphalt mat is placed on existing trackbeds, the 
track must be removed and the underlying material excavated 
to the desired grade. The asphalt mat may be built directly on 
the subgrade or a new granular base course may be constructed. 
The upper portion of old trackbeds can aiso be used as a base 
course. The asphalt mat is then placed by a standard highway 
asphalt paver and compacted by a standard roller. The track is 
then rebuilt or dragged back on the asphalt mat. For the full-
depth and overlay sections, cribbing aggregate is spread to fill 
the space between the ties and to form the shoulders so the ties 
will not slip on the asphalt mat. For the underlay sections, 
ballast is spread from railroad cars and the track is raised to 
accommodate a specified thickness of ballast under the ties. 
The ballast also fills the crib areas between the ties and 
provides the shoulders. 
The recommended asphalt mix is a slightly modified dense-
graded highway mix composed of 1- to 1.5-in. (25- to 38-mm) 
maximum sized aggregated and AC-10 or AC-20 viscosity-
graded asphalt cement. The proportions are slightly different

Approximately 30 installations, including numerous high-
way and railroad crossings, were constructed in Kentucky, 
Oklahoma, West Virginia, Massachusetts, Indiana, Louisiana, 
and Missouri. Several significant test tracks have been con-
structed since 1981 (1 ft = 0.305 m; 1 in. = 25.4 mm): 
• Seaboard System Railroad, Ravenna, Kentucky, yard, 
1981: two 500-ft-long, 12-ft-wide full-depth sections, one 8 in. 
thick, the other 12 in. thick, constructed on a curved portion of 
the main line. 
• Santa Fe Railway, Oklahoma City, Flynn yard, 1982: one 
532-ft-long, 12-ft-wide, 8-in.-thick underlay section con-
structed on a curved portion of the trim lead track. 
• Santa Fe Railway, Oklahoma City, automobile-unloading 
yard, 1982: approximately 5 acres of 4-in.-thick underlay sec-
tion with asphalt-paved driving areas between tracks. 
• Seaboard System Railroad, Conway, Kentucky, 1983: two 
1,000-ft-long, 12-ft-wide underlay sections, one 5 in. thick, the 
other 8 in. thick, constructed on the Cincinnati to Knoxville 
main line. 
• Chessie System Railroads, Deepwater, West Virginia, 
bridge approaches, 1984: two 200-ft-long, 12-ft-wide underlay 
sections, 4 in. and 8 in. thick, constructed on the Huntington to 
Hinton main line. 
The test installations have been subjected to periodic instru-
mented tests and measurements to monitor the performances 
and responses of the track system. Among the periodic mea-
surements are the moisture contents of the sub grade and the old 
roadbed under the asphalt mat, the temperature distribution 
within the trackbed, the elevations along the top of the rail, the 
stiffness or track modulus under static loading conditions, and 
the determination of geometric parameters by track geometry 
vehicles. 
103 
All installations have exhibited excellent performance. Com-
pared with that of conventional ballasted trackbeds, the mois-
ture content of the subgrade or old roadbed directly under the 
asphalt mat was lower. Moisture contents directly under the 
asphalt mats were near optimum for maximum density and 
varied only slightly from as-constructed conditions. This water-
proofing effect will provide consistent load-carrying capability 
of the subgrade, even on subgrades of marginal quality, and 
prevent the intrusion of subgrade soils into the ballast with 
subsequent fouling and pumping. The temperature fluctuations 
in the asphalt mat were minimal because of the insulative and 
temperature attenuative characteristics of the overlying ballast 
and cribbing aggregate. For the overlay at Ravenna yard, the 
maximum temperature of the asphalt mat was 35°F (1.7°C) in 
the winter and 80°F (26. 7°C) in the summer; for the underlay at 
Conway, the temperature ranged from 36°F (2°C) to 79°F 
(26°C). The absence of extreme temperatures, such as are 
experienced in highway pavements, will increase fatigue life 
during the winter and decrease permanent deformation during 
the summer. It was found that no significant changes in eleva-
tion occurred, even after several years of heavy traffic on old 
roadbeds, which had previously exhibited frequent settlements 
due to soft roadbeds and pumping. The deflections and track 
moduli of underlays were near optimum (i.e., slightly resilient 
and not overly stiff) and could be maintained for a longer 
period of time and be less affected by variations in rainfall and 
other environmental conditions than are typical ballasted 
tracks. Track geometry tests indicated that no detectable 
changes in geometric parameters had ever occurred. 
Asphalt cores were obtained from the Cleveland and New 
Mexico installations constructed during the late 1960s. Vis-
cosity and penetration tests on the recovered asphalt indicated 
no hardening of the asphalt cement and no deterioration of the 
mixtures under the insulated environment. Because asphalt 
retains its resilient characteristics for a long period of time, 
there is a significantly reduced tendency for the asphalt mat to 
become brittle and cracked. This will greatly prolong the struc-
tural life of an asphalt mat in a track structure compared with 
that revealed by data obtained on highways. 
COMPUTER MODELING 
A computer program named KENTRACK (3) was developed 
for the structural analysis and design of railroad tracks. Figure 
2 shows the various components of the track system to be 
analyzed. From top to bottom, the track is composed of rails, 
tie plates, ties, and the layered system. The finite element 
method was used in the analysis; the rails and ties were consid-
ered beam elements and the tie plates spring elements. The load 
is transmitted from the ties to the layered system through 
circular areas of equal diameter, thus Burmister's layered the-
ory, so well known in the analysis of highway pavements, can 
be applied By simply changing the properties of the layers, the 
program can be used for conventional ballasted tracks as well 
as hot-mix asphalt trackbeds. Major responses computed by the 
program include the deflections of rail, the bending and shear 
stresses in rail and tie, the contact pressure between tie and 
layered system, the horizontal tensile stress and strain at the 
bottom of hot-mix asphalt, and the vertical compressive stress

By using the critical stress or strain in the trackbed, damage 
analysis can be performed by Miner's hypothesis (4). Because 
the elastic moduli of a layered system, particularly the hot-mix 
asphalt, vary with the time of the year, each year can be divided 
into 12 months or a number of seasons for damage analysis. 
Damage, computed on a monthly or seasonal basis for given 
traffic and material properties, is accumulated up to a damage 
ratio of 1.0 using the concept of linear summation of cycle 
ratios. Two criteria, similar to those used for highway pave-
ments, are proposed for damage analysis: limiting the horizon-
tal tensile strain at the bottom of hot-mix asphalt to prevent 
fatigue cracking and limiting the vertical compressive stress on 
the top of the subgrade to reduce permanent deformation. The 
reason for using the vertical compressive stress, instead of 
compressive strain, as is done in standard highway practice, 
will be discussed later. 
The purpose of damage analysis is to determine design life. 
In highway pavements there is only one design life because the 
hot-mix asphalt must be replaced or overlaid whenever the 
design life for fatigue cracking or pavement deformation is 
reached. In railroad trackbeds there are two design lives, one 
involving the fatigue cracking of hot-mix asphalt and the other 
involving the permanent deformation of the track. The required 
design life for fatigue cracking should be much greater than 
that for permanent deformation because the latter can be cor-
rected by adjusting the ballast or shimming the rails or ties. 
When permanent deformation has been corrected, the track is 
considered new and requires further correction only when the 
new design life for permanent deformation is reached. 
To compute the stresses and strains in highway pavements, a 
program called KENLAYER was also developed. KENLAYER 
has the same capability as KENTRACK except that wheel 
ioads are appiied directiy on the iayered system through singie, 
dual, or dual-tandem circular areas. 
DESIGN CRITERIA 
Fatigue cracking and permanent deformation are the two crite-
ria used most frequently for the design of highway pavements. 
In the Asphalt Institute's design method (5), the allowable 
nwnber of load repetitions for fatigue cracking (Nc) is related 
to the horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of hot-mix asphalt

(3) 
Equations 2 and 3 are based on long years of experience and 
the analysis of AASHO Road Test data. The design system is 
based on the asphalt surface being exposed to the atmosphere, 
which accelerates oxidation and hardening of the asphalt and 
shortens fatigue life. Because of the difference in loading 
conditions, environmental effects, and performance require-
ments, these equations may not be applicable to the design of 
railroad trackbeds. However, in the absence of experience in 
railroad applications, these equations can be used as a guide. 
They should be modified as more experience is gained. The 
reason that the Shell criterion for permanent deformation is 
used, instead of the Asphalt Institute's criterion, is because it 
allows a greater number of load repetitions and is more com-
patible with the larger compressive strain under railroad load-
ings. It is believed that the use of highway failure criteria for 
the design of railroad trackbeds is quite conservative because 
the hot-mix asphalt and subgrade are better confined and insu-
lated and should offer greater resistance to fatigue cracking and 
permanent deformation. 
The use of compressive strain, instead of compressive stress, 
in Equation 3 is a convenient way to eliminate the effect of the 
stiffness or modulus of the subgrade. However, it has been 
found that the vertical compressive stress is a much better and 
more sensitive indicator of structural adequacy, particularly for 
railroad trackbeds (7). This can also be seen from Table 1 in 
which the stresses and strains in a 4-in. (102-mm) full depth are 
compared with those in an overlay composed of a 4-in. (102-
mm) hot-mix asphalt on a 4-in. (102-mm) granular base. In the 
analysis, it is assumed that the hot-mix asphalt has an elastic 
modulus of 500,000 psi (3.5 GPa) and a Poisson's ratio of 0.45 
and that the subgrade has an elastic modulus of 7,500 psi (51.7 
MPa) and a Poisson's ratio of 0.40. The granular base is 
assumed to be nonlinear with K1 of 7,500 psi and K2 of 0.5. 
The highway loading is a standard 18,000-lb (80-kN) single 
axle load with dual tires that have a contact pressure of 70 psi 
105 
(482 kPa) and a spacing of 13.5 in. (343 mm) on centers. The 
railroad loading consists of two 66,000-lb (294-kN) axle loads 
spaced 70 in. (1.78 m) apart and is applied to RE132 rails on 
wood ties spaced 20 in. (508 mm) on centers. These are the two 
axles at the end of one car. Actually, there are two more axles at 
the end of the adjacent car and these four axles should be 
grouped as a unit and considered as one load repetition. 
Because the stresses and strains under the two axles in one car 
are greater than those under the four axles in two adjoining 
cars, only two axles were used in the analysis. The considera-
tion of two axles at the end of one car, or four axles on two 
adjoining cars, as one load repetition is also quite conservative. 
When a train travels at a high speed, the stress and strain under 
one group of axle loads is not completely released before the 
application of the next loads, which results in less destructive 
effect. The elastic modulus of wood ties is assumed to be 1.5 x 
106 psi (10.3 GPa) and the tie plate stiffness is assumed to be 7 
x 106 lb/in. (791 N-m/mm). Unless noted otherwise, these 
parameters and assumptions were used for all the analysis 
presented in this paper. 
Table 1 gives the effect of 4-in. (102-mm) granular base on 
the stresses and strains in highway pavements and railroad 
trackbeds. Assuming the stress or strain in a 4-in. (102-mm) full 
depth with no base as unity, the stress and strain in a 4-in. (102-
mm) hot-mix asphalt on a 4-in. (102-mm) base is expressed as a 
fraction, as indicated by the values in parentheses. It can be 
seen that the effect of granular base in reducing the horizontal 
tensile strain is nearly the same as that in reducing the horizon-
tal tensile stress. Therefore it does not make any significant 
difference whether the horizontal tensile stress or strain is used 
as a design criterion. However, this is not the case for the 
vertical compressive stress or strain. For highway pavement, 
the addition of a 4-in. (102-mm) base reduces the vertical stress 
to 76 percent but the vertical strain to 92 percent. For railroad 
trackbed, the vertical stress is reduced to 88 percent but the 
vertical strain is increased to 106 percent. This clearly indicates 
that the vertical compressive strain is not a good indicator of 
structural adequacy because the addition of a 4-in. (102-mm) 
granular base does not decrease, but actually increases, the 
compressive strain. The reason for the increase in vertical 
compressive strain is the decrease in average lateral compres-
sive stress (Table 1).

Figure 4 shows the effect of hot-mix asphalt or base thick-
ness on the stress or strain ratios. A review of Figure 4 and 
Table 2 reveals the following: 
1. The effect of thickness on the horizontal tensile strain at 
the bottom of hot-mix asphalt is nearly the same as that on the 
horizontal tensile stress, as indicated by the close proximity of 
the two curves. Therefore either tensile strain or tensile stress 
can be used as a design criterion for fatigue cracking. Follow-
ing highway practice, the use of tensile strain is recommended 
for railroad trackbeds. 
2. An increase in the thickness of hot-mix asphalt decreases 
the tensile strain in highway pavements but not necessarily in 
railroad trackbeds. For railroad underlays with a given com-
bined thickness of ballast and hot-mix asphalt, the tensile strain 
increases as the thickness of hot-mix asphalt increases, which 
indicates that the use of ballast is more effective than the use of 
hot-mix asphalt in reducing tensile strains. That the replace-
ment of ballast by hot-mix asphalt increases the tensile strain is

3. The use of full-depth construction is effective in reducing

at the top of the subgrade is different from that on the vertical 
compressive stress, particularly for railroad trackbeds, as indi-
cated by the large spacing between the two curves. Therefore 
designs based on compressive strain are expected to be dif-
ferent from those based on compressive stress. Because com-
pressive stress is more sensitive to changes in thickness, it is 
recommended for use in the design of railroad trackbeds.

the subgrade. However, the decrease is much greater in high-
way pavements than in railroad trackbeds. This is as expected 
because highway loadings are distributed through tires over 
small areas, whereas railroad loadings are distributed through 
rails and ties over a large area.

tensile strain is due to the combined effect of larger contact 
pressures near the wheel loads, which result in greater positive 
moments, and smaller contact pressures away from the loads, 
which result in smaller negative moments. The net effect is a 
tremendous increase in bending moments, which overshadows 
the effect of increase in the thickness of hot-mix asphalt.

subgrade with a modulus of 30,000 psi (207 MPa), there is no 
way for the full-depth trackbed to achieve a fatigue life of 30 
years as recommended for fatigue cracking. The same is true 
for overlays unless the subgrade is greatly improved by soil 
stabilization or by incorporating a thick layer of granular base. 
The shorter fatigue life for the 8-in. (203-mm) full depth on a 
weak subgrade, compared with the 4-in. (102-mm) full depth, is 
due to the load concentration caused by the stiffer trackbed. If 
the track can be shimmed to adjust elevations, there should be 
no difficulty in achieving a design life of 5 years as recom-
mended for permanent deformations. If the track cannot be 
shimmed and the design life for permanent deformation should 
also be 30 years, the required design life will be more difficult 
to obtain. Because of the high tensile strain at the bottom of 
hot-mix asphalt and the inapplicability of existing railroad 
maintenance procedures, the use of full depth and overlay for 
heavy-haul trackbeds is not recommended. 
Figure Sb shows that even underlays with a 4-in. (102-mm) 
hot-mix asphalt can still be made to achieve a fatigue life of 30 
years by simply increasing the thickness of ballast. Also there 
is no difficulty in achieving a design life of 5 years for perma-
nent deformation. The use of 5 years for design life is reason-
able because any permanent deformations can be easily cor-
rected by adjusting the ballast during routine maintenance. 
It can be seen that, from both the design and maintenance 
viewpoints, an nnderlay is far superior to an overlay because 
the required hot-mix asphalt is much thinner and the existing 
railroad maintenance method can still be applied. 
UNDERLAYS VERSUS CONVENTIONAL TRACKBEDS 
Because of the better load-carrying characteristics of hot-mix 
asphalt, the combined thickness of ballast and hot-mix asphalt 
in an underlay should be smaller than that of ballast and 
subballast in a conventional trackbed. It was found that a 
conventional trackbed with 8-in. (203-mm) ballast and 6-in. 
(152-mm) subballast is initially equivalent to an underlay with 
deformation 
8-in. (203-mm) ballast and 4-in. (102-mm) hot-mix asphalt. 
This equivalency is based on the vertical compressive stress on 
the top of the subgrade as given in Table 3. It is assumed that 
the ballast, subballast, and subgrade in the conventional track-
bed remain separated without pumping, a condition difficult to 
achieve in reality. The compressive stresses were determined 
by KENTRACK using the geometry and material parameters 
described previously. The allowable number of load repetitions 
was computed by Equation 4. Four different moduli of sub-
grade were used. In the conventional trackbeds, the subballast 
was considered nonlinear with K1 = 3,750 psi, K2 = 0.5, and a 
Poisson's ratio of 0.35. In the underlays, three different moduli 
were assumed for the hot-mix asphalt. 
It can be seen from Table 3 that the conventional trackbed 
and the hot-mix asphalt underlay are equivalent because the 
compressive stress in the conventional trackbed lies between 
the extreme values shown for the underlay. The comparison is 
based on the assumption that both systems have the same 
modulus of subgrade. Because of the waterproofing effect of 
hot-mix asphalt, the modulus of subgrade in the underlay will 
be kept intact, while that in the conventional trackbed will be 
lowered as the moisture content increases. If the modulus of 
subgrade is reduced from 7,500 psi (5.17 MPa) to 3,000 psi 
(20.7 MPa), the compressive stress in the conventional track-
bed will be reduced from 11.l to 8.2 psi (77 to 57 kPa) but the 
allowable number of load repetitions will be reduced from 
463,000 to 53,800. In this case the design life of an underlay 
with 8-in. (203-mm) ballast and 4-in. (102-mm) hot-mix 
asphalt is more than eight times greater than that of a conven-
tional trackbed with 8-in. (203-mm) ballast and 6-in. (152-mm) 
subballast. 
CONCLUSIONS 
The design, construction, and performance of hot-mix asphalt 
railroad trackbeds are presented. The excellent performance of 
some 30 experimental sections constructed so far has offered 

110 
the railroad industry a timely and viable option for reducing 
trackbed maintenance costs and improving train operating effi-
ciency. On the basis of the critical stresses and strains in 
highway pavements and railroad trackbeds and the application 
of highway failure criteria, the following general conclusions 
can be drawn: 
1. Similar to highway pavements, the design of hot-mix 
asphalt trackbeds should consider both fatigue cracking and 
permanent deformation. The fatigue cracking can be based on 
the horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of hot-mix asphalt,

compressive stress on the top of the subgrade. 
2. In the design of railroad trackbeds, there are two separate 
design lives: one that requires the replacement or rehabilitation 
of hot-mix asphalt that has suffered fatigue cracking and 
another that requires the adjustment of track that has experi-
enced permanent deformation. In the design of highway pave-
ments, there is only one design life because both fatigue crack-
ing and permanent deformation occur in the hot-mix asphalt 
and whichever has a lesser life controls the design. 
3. Because of the differences in loading conditions, environ-
mental effects, and performance requirements, the failure crite-
ria for highway pavements may not be applicable to railroad 
trackbeds. Given the lack of railroad data, highway criteria can 
only be used as a guide and should be revised as more experi-
ence is gained. The analysis by KENTRACK shows that under-
lays can be designed economically to satisfy the highway 
failure criteria. It is believed that the use of highway failure 
criteria is quite conservative because the hot-mix asphalt and 
subgrade in a railroad trackbed are better confined and insu-
lated and the railroad loadings are repeated at shorter intervals. 
4. Increasing the thickness of hot-mix asphalt is not as 
effective in reducing the critical stress and strain in railroad 
trackbeds as in highway pavements. The requirement of a very 
thick hot-mix asphalt to reduce the horizontal tensile strain 
makes it uneconomical to use full depth or overlays for heavy-
haul trackbeds. 
5. A direct comparison of predicted design life for conven-
tional trackbeds and asphalt trackbeds must consider the effect 
of lowering, over time, of the subgrade modulus of the conven-
tional trackbed, which is caused by the increased moisture 
content of the subgrade. Also, as the subgrade mixes with the 
ballast, the ballast modulus is decreased substantially. These 
effects decrease the number of allowable load repetitions for 
conventional trackbeds. Because the asphait iayer separates the 
ballast from the subgrade and provides a drier subgrade, 
optimum subgrade and ballast qualities will be maintained. 
6. From both design and maintenance viewpoints, underlays 
are far superior to overlays. Both failure criteria can be easily 
satisfied by increasing the thickness of ballast. 
TRANSPORTATION RESEARCH RECORD 1095 
7. In designing underlays, the use of a thick layer of hot-mix 
asphalt is not warranted. For a given combined thickness of 
ballast and hot-mix asphalt, the thicker the hot-mix asphalt, the 
shorter the fatigue life and the greater the contact pressure 
between tie and ballast. Therefore the use of a thin layer of hot-
mix asphalt, say 3 to 4 in. (76 to 102 mm), with a thick layer of 
ballast, say 8 in. (203 mm) or more, is recommended. 
8. The main function of hot-mix asphalt underlays is to 
waterproof the subgrade and thus provide consistent load-
carrying capability for the trackbed even on marginal sub-
grades. The asphalt mat will confine the ballast and eliminate
